title: If they didn't laugh
hook: when the foolish hear of the Tao they laugh, and without their laughter it wouldn't be the Tao (Tao Te Ching 41)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the way returns: the Tao goes out and comes back, and yields as it goes. Your line was returning. What did you come back to, and how did it feel to pick it up again? Day one thousand one hundred three.

Someone at work sees you sit with your eyes closed for a minute at your desk and asks, half joking, whether you've fallen asleep. Or a cousin at a family dinner raises an eyebrow at the morning walk, the candle, the phone left in another room. A small laugh. Not cruel, just puzzled. Chapter forty-one of the Tao Te Ching saw that laugh coming, and it treats the laugh as something other than a problem.
screen: `EYES CLOSED AT A DESK.` → `A PUZZLED LAUGH.` → `CHAPTER FORTY-ONE SAW IT COMING.`

segments.voice: First, three hearers. The chapter opens with three kinds of people hearing about the way. The first hears and puts it into practice with everything they have. The second hears, and seems to keep it one day and lose it the next. The third hears it and laughs out loud. Second, the twist. In James Legge's translation the chapter says of that laugh: "If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao." The laugh isn't treated as a problem to fix. It's treated almost as a sign. If the way made perfect sense to everyone at first glance, it wouldn't be the way. Third, why it looks funny. The chapter goes straight on to a list of things that look like their opposites: the bright way seems dim, the way forward seems to go back, the level way seems rough. Seen from outside, slowing down looks like falling behind, and sitting still looks like doing nothing. Of course someone laughs. Notice what the chapter doesn't do. It doesn't tell anyone to argue with the laughers, or to look down on them. It just says the laugh comes with the territory. Fourth, the middle hearer. Keeping a practice for a week, then dropping it the first time somebody smirks: that's the middle hearer's pattern. Chapter forty-one offers that hearer something steadying. The laugh doesn't prove you're wrong. It may only prove that what you're doing looks, from the outside, like nothing.
screen: `THREE HEARERS.` · `NO LAUGH, NO TAO.` · `IT LOOKS LIKE ITS OPPOSITE.` · `THE MIDDLE HEARER.` · then, large: `IF THEY DIDN'T LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a practice others find odd. Choose the small one you already have, or the one you've been shy about. This sit counts. Settle where you are. If anyone near you could see, let them see. Let a little self-consciousness rise, the feeling of being watched doing something that looks like nothing, and don't push it away. Just keep sitting through it. If you pray, this can be a quiet prayer. If you don't, it can be two minutes of breathing on purpose. The bell holds the time.
If they didn't laugh. Chapter forty-one: when some people hear of the way, they laugh, and if they didn't, it wouldn't be the way. Today's word.
Your line: they laugh. If someone smiles at your quiet minute or your odd little habit today, let it be, and keep it anyway. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often quote chapter forty-one when a practice like stillness or simplicity draws puzzled looks, taking the laugh as part of the path rather than a reason to quit.

myth: chapter forty-one tells readers to argue with those who laugh
it just says the laugh comes with the territory.
the chapter says the way forward can seem to go back
it lists things that look like their opposites.
in the chapter, only one kind of person hears of the way
there are three hearers: one practices, one wavers, one laughs.

fork.setup: you've kept a quiet morning minute for a week. a friend laughs and calls it weird. what does chapter forty-one suggest?
options: drop it, since it looks odd.
keep it, and let the laugh be.
fork.reveal: the chapter says that if the way weren't laughed at, it wouldn't be the way. it doesn't ask you to win the argument.

original.note: Chinese: to laugh; in chapter forty-one, what the third hearer does on hearing of the Tao.

trapdoor: what you thought: if people laugh at it, maybe it's silly.
what it means: the chapter treats the laugh almost as a sign. what looks like nothing from outside may be the way.
what a scholar hears: Legge's 'if it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao', followed by a list of things that seem their opposite.

notes: Editor: hook no longer implies an age ('a very long time ago') or tells the listener what they expect; replaced the stock 'an ordinary Tuesday' frame with 'the middle hearer'.
Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 41 word for word, including '(thus)'.
Legge names the three hearers 'scholars of the highest/middle/lowest class'; the script avoids the class language and calls them three hearers. Confirm that paraphrase is fair.

The paradox list (bright seems dim, forward seems back, level seems rough) is paraphrased from ch. 41; day 1107 (ch. 45, 'seems clumsy') takes up a similar pattern, so this day touches it only briefly.
The office and family-dinner scenes are the writer's illustrations, not the text's.
